set1.q: Where does Histoplasma capsulatum grow in nature?
opts: Cool, humid soils of South America

Cool, humid soils of Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and Paraguay are where Paracoccidioides brasiliensis lives. Histoplasma grows in moist soil rich in nitrogen, especially with bird and bat guano.
Decaying plants, pine straw and hay

Decaying plant matter, pine straw and hay bales are the haunts of Sporothrix schenckii, a saprobe that enters through puncture wounds. Histoplasma's home is moist, nitrogen-rich soil with bird and bat guano.
Moist, nitrogen-rich soil with guano

Correct. Histoplasma capsulatum grows in moist soil with a high nitrogen content, especially soil containing bird and bat guano. When wind or digging disturbs that soil, the conidia become airborne and are inhaled.
Alkaline, salty soil of hot, dry land

Alkaline, salty soil in semiarid, hot climates is the home of Coccidioides immitis, whose spread is boosted by drought, heavy rain and windstorms. Histoplasma needs moist, nitrogen-rich soil, especially with guano.

set1.q: To what practice can the resistance of Aspergillus to azole fungicides be attributed?
opts: Long topical courses for ringworm
Topical azoles for several weeks are the usual treatment for dermatophytoses, but they are not where Aspergillus resistance is traced. That resistance is attributed to agricultural crop spraying.
Amphotericin B in transplant care
Amphotericin B is not an azole; it forms complexes with fungal cell membrane lipids. Aspergillus resistance to azole fungicides is attributed to agricultural crop spraying.
Agricultural crop spraying
Correct. Aspergillus is a very common airborne soil fungus, and its resistance to azole fungicides can be attributed to agricultural practices: spraying crops to prevent losses due to fungi.
Hospital disinfectant overuse

Partial resistance to common disinfectants is a trait of Candida auris that keeps its hospital outbreaks going. Azole resistance in Aspergillus, an airborne soil fungus, traces to agricultural crop spraying.

set1.q: How is tinea pedis mainly spread?
opts: Puncture by thorns or splinters

A thorn or splinter puncture introduces subcutaneous fungi such as Sporothrix schenckii into deeper tissue. Tinea pedis is a cutaneous infection of the keratinized skin of the foot, picked up from public surfaces.
Going barefoot as a daily habit
Tinea pedis is rare where people usually go barefoot, so daily bare feet are not its source. It spreads by exposure to public surfaces and settles between the digits and on the soles.
Exposure to public surfaces

Correct. Tinea pedis (foot) and tinea manuum (hand) are spread by exposure to public surfaces and occur between the digits and on the soles. Tellingly, tinea pedis is rare where people usually go barefoot, so it is the shared surfaces, not bare feet, that matter.
Contact with infected animals
Contact with animals is the main source of tinea barbae, ringworm of the chin and beard of adult males. The foot form, tinea pedis, comes from exposure to public surfaces.

set1.q: Which traits make hospital outbreaks of Candida auris hard to eradicate?
opts: Switching between mold and yeast forms

Switching between a mold at 30 C and a yeast at 37 C is thermal dimorphism, the adaptation of the true fungal pathogens to the human host. Candida auris outbreaks persist because of drug resistance, heat tolerance and partial disinfectant resistance.
Drug, heat and disinfectant resistance

Correct. Candida auris is emerging as a serious cause of invasive candidiasis, with hospital outbreaks that are difficult to eradicate: it shows antifungal drug resistance, is thermoresistant and is partially resistant to common disinfectants. It was first identified in an ear infection, hence its name.
A capsule shown by negative stain

An encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain is Cryptococcus neoformans, and capsules are a fungal virulence factor. Candida auris outbreaks persist because the yeast resists antifungal drugs, tolerates heat and partly resists common disinfectants.
Arthroconidia spread by windstorms

Windstorms after cycles of drought and heavy rain spread Coccidioides from alkaline, salty soils in hot, semiarid climates. Candida auris is a hospital problem whose outbreaks resist eradication through drug, heat and partial disinfectant resistance.

set1.q: A student who shares bedding develops inflamed, red ring-shaped lesions on the smooth skin of the trunk. Which name fits this ringworm?
opts: Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis involves the scalp and hair-bearing regions of the head, may cause hair loss and is common in children. Rings on the smooth skin of the trunk are tinea corporis.
Tinea unguium
Tinea unguium is a persistent colonization of the nails of the hands and feet that distorts the nail bed. Inflamed, red rings on smooth skin after shared bedding are tinea corporis.
Tinea corporis

Correct. Tinea corporis, ringworm of the body, occurs as inflamed, red ring lesions anywhere on smooth skin and spreads by contact, clothing and bedding. Rings on smooth trunk skin after shared bedding are the decisive clues.
Tinea cruris

Tinea cruris (jock itch) affects the groin and scrotal regions and is pervasive among athletes and in crowded living conditions. Ring lesions on smooth skin elsewhere, such as the trunk, are tinea corporis.

set1.q: A yeast isolate incubated in serum for 2 to 4 hours grows short hyphal sprouts. Which identification test is this?
opts: Hair infection test
The hair infection test inoculates sterile hair with culture isolates from hair, skin and nail specimens; it does not use serum. Hyphal sprouts from yeasts in serum define the germ tube test.
Test for dimorphism

Dimorphism is tested by growing an isolate at two temperatures (room temperature, 25 or 30 C, against 37 C) to show the mold and yeast forms, not by a few hours in serum. Short hyphal sprouts in serum are germ tubes.
Periodic acid-Schiff stain
Periodic acid-Schiff is a stain used on hair, skin and nail specimens; it colors fungal elements but makes nothing sprout. Hyphal tubes from yeasts in serum define the germ tube test.
Germ tube test

Correct. Some yeasts, when incubated in serum for 2 to 4 hours, sprout tiny hyphal tubes called germ tubes. The germ tube test sits among the identification tests for isolates from blood, cerebrospinal fluid, pus and vaginal secretions, alongside differential media and biochemical and antigen tests.

set1.q: Into what form do inhaled Blastomyces conidia convert in the lungs?
opts: Spherules full of endospores
Spherules filled with endospores are what Coccidioides forms in the lungs after its arthrospores are inhaled. Blastomyces conidia convert to yeasts instead, and the yeasts multiply there.
Branched septate hyphae
Hyphae are the mold form of the natural habitat below 30 C, and branched septate hyphae in sputum are typical of Aspergillus. At body temperature Blastomyces converts to multiplying yeasts.
Block-like arthroconidia

Block-like arthroconidia are the free-living form of Coccidioides, the form inhaled from dust; they are not a lung form of either fungus. Inhaled Blastomyces conidia become yeasts that multiply in the lungs.
Multiplying yeast cells

Correct. Blastomyces is a dimorphic fungus, free-living in soil; its inhaled conidia convert to yeasts that multiply in the lungs, the yeast phase that dimorphic fungi adopt at body temperature in an animal host.

set1.q: Why is immunization typically ineffective for preventing fungal infections?
opts: Reinfection is exceedingly common

Correct. Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common. Control therefore relies on antifungal drugs (amphotericin B, flucytosine, azoles and nystatin), surgical removal of damaged tissue where needed, and limiting contact with spores.
Fungi cause too few human infections

Fungi are relatively nonpathogenic, yet they still cause the dermatophytoses (the most prevalent fungal diseases), fatal systemic disease and a rising share of nosocomial infections. The stated reason vaccines fail is that reinfection is exceedingly common.
Fungi turn into yeasts inside the host

Thermal dimorphism, the switch to yeasts at body temperature, is a survival adaptation of true pathogens, not the reason given for vaccine failure. Immunization is ineffective because reinfection is exceedingly common.
Antifungal drugs already prevent infection

Antifungal drugs such as amphotericin B, flucytosine, azoles and nystatin treat infection; they are not the means of prevention. Prevention is limited to respirator masks and protective clothing, and vaccines fail because reinfection is so common.

set1.q: Blastomyces dermatitidis lies dormant in warm, dry weather. When does it sporulate?
opts: In colder, wetter weather

Correct. Blastomyces is dormant in warm, dry weather and sporulates in the colder, wetter weather that follows, releasing the conidia that people inhale. This cycle plays out in the soils of the midwestern and southeastern United States and southern Canada.
In hot, dry summer weather

Warm, dry weather is when Blastomyces lies dormant, not when it sporulates; the season is reversed. Sporulation follows in colder, wetter weather across its midwestern, southeastern and southern Canadian range.
After drought, rain and windstorms
Cycles of drought and heavy rain followed by windstorms drive the spread of Coccidioides in hot, semiarid climates with alkaline, salty soil. Blastomyces sporulates in colder, wetter weather.
Inside the host at body heat

At body temperature a dimorphic fungus is in its parasitic yeast phase, reproducing by budding; sporulation belongs to the mold phase of the natural habitat. In soil, Blastomyces sporulates in colder, wetter weather.

set1.q: Sporothrix schenckii is a saprobic fungus. What does saprobic mean?
opts: It feeds on dead or decaying matter

Correct. A saprobe derives its nutrition from dead or decaying matter. Sporothrix schenckii is a very common saprobic fungus that decomposes plant matter in soil, which is why thorns, wood, bare roots, pine straw and hay carry it to people.
It must live on a living host

Most fungal pathogens do not require a host to complete their life cycles, and a saprobe lives free in nature. Sporothrix schenckii decomposes plant matter in soil and infects people only incidentally, through puncture wounds.
It switches from mold to yeast at 37 C

Growing as a mold at 30 C and as a yeast at 37 C is thermal dimorphism, the most striking adaptation of true fungal pathogens, not the meaning of saprobic. A saprobe feeds on dead or decaying matter, as Sporothrix does on plant matter in soil.
It lives as normal flora on human skin

Living as normal flora of the mouth, genitalia, large intestine or skin describes Candida albicans, whose infections are usually endogenous. A saprobe such as Sporothrix schenckii lives in soil on dead or decaying plant matter.

set1.q: How do mycotoxicoses usually arise?
opts: Fungi invading through broken skin
Fungi entering through traumatized skin cause subcutaneous mycoses such as sporotrichosis, which are infections. Mycotoxicoses are intoxications by fungal toxins that are ingested or inhaled.
Spores provoking a hypersensitivity

Fungal spores provoking hypersensitivity, as in farmer's lung, cause atopic allergies, a separate category. Mycotoxicoses are poisonings by fungal toxins taken in by ingestion or inhalation, such as aflatoxin and ergot.
Overgrowth of resident yeast flora

Overgrowth of resident yeast is the usual, endogenous origin of Candida albicans infection. A mycotoxicosis is an intoxication: the person ingests or inhales a fungal toxin, as with aflatoxin or ergot.
Ingesting or inhaling fungal toxins

Correct. Mycotoxicoses are usually caused by ingesting or inhaling fungal toxins. Examples are aflatoxin on grains, corn and peanuts and ergot on rye or other grains contaminated by Claviceps fungi; they are intoxications, not infections.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which community measure reduces inhalation of Coccidioides spores in an endemic area?
opts: Oiling roads to keep down dust

Correct. Coccidioides arthrospores are inhaled from dust, so prevention targets dust: oiling roads, planting to minimize erosion and using dust masks. Farming, road construction or repair, archaeological digs, landslides and dust storms all raise exposure.
Vaccinating outdoor workers

Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common. Coccidioides is prevented by limiting dust: oiling roads, planting against erosion and dust masks.
Isolating Valley fever patients
Coccidioides is caught from soil dust, and most fungal infections are not communicable, so isolating patients does nothing to stop exposure. Dust control, such as oiling roads, does.
Clearing pigeon roosts from buildings

Soil around urban pigeon roosts harbors Cryptococcus neoformans, and bird droppings enrich Histoplasma's soil. Coccidioides lives in alkaline, salty, semiarid soil and is prevented by dust control such as oiling roads.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which fungi naturally inhabit the human body and can pass person to person or by fomites such as shared exercise equipment?
opts: Dermatophytes and Candida

Correct. Unlike most fungal pathogens, which need no host and are generally not communicable, dermatophytes (literally 'skin plants') and Candida naturally inhabit the human body and are transmissible from person to person or by fomites such as shared exercise equipment.
Histoplasma and Blastomyces

These are soil fungi: Histoplasma grows in moist soil rich in bird and bat guano, Blastomyces in forest soil, decaying wood and manure. Both are caught by inhaling conidia, and histoplasmosis is not transmitted person to person.
Coccidioides and Paracoccidioides

Both live in soil (Coccidioides in alkaline, salty soil of hot, semiarid climates; Paracoccidioides in cool, humid soil) and are caught by inhaling spores or, for Paracoccidioides, inoculating them into skin. They are not residents of the body.
Aspergillus and Cryptococcus

Aspergillus is an airborne soil fungus and Cryptococcus inhabits soil around pigeon roosts and soil with decaying wood; both come from the environment, not from other people. The body-dwelling, transmissible fungi are dermatophytes and Candida.

set1.q: On what basis do most scientists now classify Pneumocystis as a fungus rather than a protozoan?
opts: Its antibody titers
Antibody titers show that human contact with Pneumocystis is very widespread and mostly asymptomatic; they do not show whether it is a fungus. The classification rests on genetic analysis.
Its genetic analysis

Correct. The taxonomy of Pneumocystis is still debated, fungus or protozoan, but most scientists lean toward a fungal classification because of genetic analysis. Its usual drugs do not settle the question: one is an antiprotozoal and the other an antibacterial.
Its response to antifungals

Pneumocystis is treated with pentamidine (antiprotozoal) and co-trimoxazole (antibacterial), which are not traditional antifungal drugs, so drug response cannot be the basis. Genetic analysis is what places it among the fungi.
Its growth as hyphae
Pneumocystis is a small, unicellular fungus, seen in tissue as cysts containing several bodies, not as hyphae. Its fungal classification rests on genetic analysis.

set1.q: A negative stain of a specimen shows encapsulated budding yeast. Which organism does this demonstrate?
opts: Candida albicans
Candida albicans also buds, but its presumptive diagnosis rests on budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae, not a capsule. The capsule outlined by a negative stain marks Cryptococcus neoformans.
Aspergillus fumigatus
Aspergillus is seen as branched septate hyphae, for example in a sputum specimen, not as a budding yeast. An encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain is Cryptococcus neoformans.
Pneumocystis jirovecii
Pneumocystis jirovecii is a small, unicellular fungus seen in tissue as cysts containing several bodies. Encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain is Cryptococcus neoformans.
Cryptococcus neoformans

Correct. A negative stain demonstrating encapsulated budding yeast is the picture of Cryptococcus neoformans, the widespread encapsulated yeast of pigeon-roost soil. Biochemical and serological testing are the best diagnostic tools for it.

set1.q: A fungal infection involves the stratum corneum and occasionally the upper dermis, but no deeper. What level of invasion is this?
opts: Superficial

Superficial involvement is an extremely shallow colonization of the epidermis, the shallowest of the three skin depths. Reaching the stratum corneum and, at times, the upper dermis is one level deeper: cutaneous.
Subcutaneous

Subcutaneous involvement occurs after a puncture wound has carried the fungus deeper, into the subcutaneous tissue below the dermis. An infection that stops at the stratum corneum and upper dermis is cutaneous.
Systemic

In systemic (deep) mycoses the fungus spreads from the lungs or other sites into the circulation, and fungemia infects the brain, kidneys and other organs. An infection limited to the stratum corneum and upper dermis is cutaneous.
Cutaneous

Correct. Cutaneous involvement takes in the stratum corneum and occasionally the upper dermis. It is deeper than the extremely shallow epidermal colonization of superficial infection but stops short of the subcutaneous tissue reached after a puncture wound.

set1.q: How can Fusarium reach and infect the eye?
opts: Spread from the nose in diabetes

Invasion of the nose, eyes, heart and brain in people with diabetes, leukemia or malnutrition is the pattern of mucormycosis from Rhizopus and Mucor. Fusarium reaches the eye through contaminated contact lenses.
Eating grain contaminated by it

Eating grains, corn or peanuts contaminated by fungi causes mycotoxicoses such as aflatoxin poisoning, an intoxication rather than an eye infection. Fusarium infects the eye through contaminated contact lenses.
Through contaminated contact lenses

Correct. Fusarium species, a mainly tropical soil mold, occasionally infect the eyes, for example through contaminated contact lenses, as well as toenails, feet and burned skin, and can result in severe disability and death.
From close person-to-person contact

Most fungal infections are not communicable; person-to-person spread is the pattern of the dermatophytes and Candida, which live on the human body. Fusarium, a soil mold, reaches the eye through contaminated contact lenses.

set1.q: Antibiotic therapy and catheters predispose patients to which opportunistic fungus?
opts: Fusarium species

Fusarium is a mainly tropical soil mold that infects eyes through contaminated contact lenses, toenails, feet and burned skin. Antibiotic therapy and catheters are the predisposing conditions tied to Candida.
Candida species

Correct. Among the common opportunistic fungi, Candida is the one associated with antibiotic therapy and catheters, alongside diabetes, corticosteroids and immunosuppression. It is the dominant opportunistic pathogen and its infections are usually endogenous.
Aspergillus species

Aspergillus is associated with leukemia, corticosteroids, tuberculosis, immunosuppression and intravenous drug abuse, not with antibiotic therapy or catheters. Those two predisposing conditions belong to Candida.
Cryptococcus species
Cryptococcus is associated with diabetes, tuberculosis, cancer, corticosteroids and immunosuppression. Antibiotic therapy and catheters are the predisposing conditions tied to Candida.

set1.q: At which temperature does a thermally dimorphic fungus grow as unicellular yeast?

25 C is room temperature, used for selective agar cultures that show the mold phase when the laboratory demonstrates dimorphism. The unicellular yeast form appears at 37 C, human body temperature.
30 C is the temperature at which dimorphic fungi grow as multicellular molds. They switch to unicellular yeasts at 37 C, human body temperature, inside the 35 to 40 C range of the animal habitat.

Correct. Thermally dimorphic fungi grow as multicellular molds at 30 C and as unicellular yeasts at 37 C, human body temperature; in the animal habitat (35 to 40 C) they live as parasitic, budding yeasts. Culturing at room temperature and at 37 C demonstrates the switch.

set1.q: Which factor may lead to white or black piedra?
opts: Poor hygiene, such as oily hair products

Correct. Both piedras are considered non-contagious and may result from poor personal hygiene, such as oily hair products and tight hats or veils. They are superficial mycoses of the hair shaft, and neither is common in the United States.
Close contact with an infected person

Both piedras are considered non-contagious, so close contact with an infected person is not how they arise. Person-to-person spread is a feature of the dermatophytes and Candida, which live on the human body.
Handling infected household animals

Animals are the main source of tinea barbae, a dermatophytosis of the chin and beard. The piedras are non-contagious and are linked to poor hygiene, such as oily hair products and tight hats or veils.
Inhaling spores from bird guano
Spores from soil rich in bird and bat guano are inhaled in histoplasmosis, a lung infection. The piedras sit on the hair shaft and are linked to poor hygiene: oily hair products, tight hats or veils.

set1.q: On the World Health Organization's fungal priority list, which fungus is ranked one tier above Coccidioides?

Correct. Coccidioides is in the medium priority group; Histoplasma species are in the high priority group, one tier above, with other Candida species, Fusarium, the eumycetoma agents and the Mucorales. The critical group sits above both.
Paracoccidioides species

Paracoccidioides species share the medium priority group with Coccidioides, Cryptococcus gattii and Pneumocystis jirovecii, so they sit level with it, not above. Histoplasma species are one tier up, in the high group.
Pneumocystis jirovecii

Pneumocystis jirovecii, the most prominent opportunistic infection in human immunodeficiency virus infection and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, is nonetheless medium priority, level with Coccidioides. Histoplasma is one tier above.
Cryptococcus gattii

Cryptococcus gattii is medium priority, level with Coccidioides, even though its relative Cryptococcus neoformans tops the critical group. Histoplasma species sit one tier above Coccidioides, in the high group.

set1.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which measure is the main way to prevent fungal infection by reducing contact with fungal spores?
opts: Routine antifungal vaccination

Immunization is typically ineffective for fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common. Prevention relies on respirator masks, protective clothing and hygiene to cut contact with spores.
Preventive amphotericin B

Amphotericin B is a highly toxic, often expensive treatment, nicknamed 'ampho-terrible' for its side effects, not a preventive measure. Prevention is limited to respirator masks, protective clothing and hygiene.
Isolating infected patients

Most fungal infections are not communicable, because the fungi need no host to complete their life cycles, so isolating patients does little. Exposure to spores is reduced with respirator masks and protective clothing.
High-quality respirator masks

Correct. Methods of prevention are essentially limited to wearing high-quality respirator masks and protective clothing, with hygiene, to reduce contact with fungal spores; the primary mycoses are caught by inhaling spores from the air. Immunization is typically ineffective.

set1.q: Which treatment is used for systemic sporotrichosis?

Pentamidine, an antiprotozoal, and co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), an antibacterial, treat Pneumocystis pneumonia and are not traditional antifungals. Systemic sporotrichosis is treated with the antifungals amphotericin B and/or itraconazole.
Topical azoles and debridement

Topical azoles for several weeks, sometimes with debridement or ultraviolet light, treat dermatophytoses that stay in keratinized skin. A systemic fungal infection needs systemic drugs: amphotericin B and/or itraconazole for sporotrichosis.
Amphotericin B and/or itraconazole

Correct. Systemic sporotrichosis is treated with amphotericin B and/or itraconazole. Heat packs and/or super-saturated potassium iodide are the treatment given for infection of the appendages and lungs; once the disease is systemic, the drug pair is used.
Heat packs and/or potassium iodide

Heat packs and/or super-saturated potassium iodide are the treatment given for sporotrichosis of the appendages and lungs. For the systemic infection asked about here, the choice is amphotericin B and/or itraconazole.

set1.q: Which description fits paracoccidioidomycosis?
opts: An opportunist needing impaired defenses
Paracoccidioides is a primary (true) fungal pathogen of rural farm workers, not an opportunist defined by impaired defenses. It causes the rarest primary mycosis, usually mild and self-limiting.
Rarest primary mycosis, usually mild

Correct. Paracoccidioidomycosis, endemic in Central and South America (mainly the cool, humid soils of Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and Paraguay), is the rarest of the primary mycoses; systemic disease is not common, and infections are usually mild and self-limiting.
Commonest primary mycosis, usually mild

Mildness is right, but rarity is reversed: the most common true fungal pathogen is Histoplasma capsulatum, cause of 'Ohio Valley fever', while Paracoccidioides causes the rarest of the primary mycoses.
Rarest primary mycosis, usually systemic
Rarity is right, but severity is overstated: systemic paracoccidioidomycosis is not common. Lung or skin infections, from inhaled or inoculated spores, are usually mild and self-limiting.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: Which ability defines a true (primary) fungal pathogen?
opts: Staying a mold at human body temperature

This reverses thermal dimorphism: these fungi grow as molds at 30 C but switch to yeasts at 37 C, human body temperature. The switch is their adaptation to the host; the defining ability is invading and growing in a healthy host.
Invading and growing in a healthy host

Correct. A true or primary fungal pathogen can invade and grow in a healthy host. Its most striking adaptation is the switch from hyphal cells to yeast cells with the change to host temperature. An opportunist, by contrast, has little or no virulence of its own and needs impaired host defenses.
Needing impaired host defenses to infect

Needing impaired defenses (human immunodeficiency virus infection, cancer, diabetes) describes an opportunistic fungal pathogen, which has little or no virulence of its own. A true pathogen needs no such help: it invades and grows in a healthy host.
Spreading readily from person to person

Most fungal pathogens do not need a host to complete their life cycles, so their infections are generally not communicable; the person-to-person spreaders are the dermatophytes and Candida, which live on the body. A true pathogen is defined by invading a healthy host.

set1.q: A wrestler living in a crowded dormitory has ringworm of the groin and scrotal skin. Which name fits?
opts: Tinea cruris

Correct. Tinea cruris, the jock itch, affects the groin and scrotal regions and is pervasive among athletes and in crowded living conditions. An athlete in crowded housing with groin and scrotal involvement fits it exactly.
Tinea pedis
Tinea pedis is ringworm of the foot, between the digits and on the soles, spread by exposure to public surfaces. Ringworm of the groin and scrotum is tinea cruris.
Tinea barbae

Tinea barbae affects the chin and beard of adult males and comes mainly from animals, not from crowded living. The groin and scrotal regions, in an athlete sharing close quarters, are the territory of tinea cruris.
Tinea manuum
Tinea manuum is ringworm of the hand, spread like tinea pedis by public surfaces and found between the digits and on the soles. Groin and scrotal ringworm in a crowded-living athlete is tinea cruris.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: A dye-stained sputum specimen shows a mass of branched septate hyphae and no yeast cells. Which fungus does this fit?
opts: Coccidioides immitis
In the lungs Coccidioides forms spherules containing endospores, and in soil block-like arthroconidia; neither is a mass of branched septate hyphae in sputum. That pattern is Aspergillus.
Aspergillus species

Correct. Branched septate hyphae in a sputum specimen are the picture of Aspergillus, an airborne soil fungus whose spores germinate in the lungs and can form fungal balls. Dyes amplify these fungal elements in tissue specimens.
Candida albicans

Candida albicans appears as budding or germinating yeast cells with young hyphae or pseudohyphae, typically from an oral or vaginal swab. A sputum mass of branched septate hyphae with no yeast cells fits Aspergillus.
Cryptococcus neoformans
Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated budding yeast shown by a negative stain, not a mass of hyphae. Branched septate hyphae without any yeast cells point to Aspergillus, an airborne soil mold.

mis.Candida albicans: germinating yeast confused with septate hyphae
mis.Cryptococcus neoformans: encapsulated yeast confused with a mold

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: How does Pneumocystis pneumonia become rapidly fatal when it is not controlled?
opts: Spherules with endospores form nodules

Spherules containing endospores and lung nodules come from inhaled Coccidioides arthrospores, and most such cases need no treatment at all. Pneumocystis pneumonia is deadly because its secretions block breathing.
Spread to the meninges and brain
Dissemination to the meninges and brain is how Cryptococcus neoformans causes severe neurological disturbance and death. Pneumocystis does its damage in the lungs, where secretions block breathing.
Secretions in the lungs block breathing
Correct. Pneumocystis pneumonia forms secretions in the lungs that block breathing; with cough, fever, shallow respiration and cyanosis, it can be rapidly fatal if not controlled with medication.
Fungal balls form in the lungs
Fungal balls form when Aspergillus spores germinate in the lungs, and invasive aspergillosis can add necrotic pneumonia. Pneumocystis kills by filling the lungs with secretions that block breathing.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: In an immunocompromised patient, where does Cryptococcus neoformans spread after the lungs, with the gravest results?
opts: The nail beds of hands and feet

Persistent colonization of the nails of the hands and feet, distorting the nail bed, is tinea unguium, a dermatophyte infection. Cryptococcus neoformans disseminates from the lungs to the meninges and brain.
The meninges and brain

Correct. Lung infection by Cryptococcus neoformans brings cough, fever and lung nodules; dissemination to the meninges and the brain can cause severe neurological disturbance and death in compromised hosts.
Nearby lymph nodes

Spread from a skin nodule to nearby lymph nodes is the lymphocutaneous form of sporotrichosis, which starts at a puncture wound. Cryptococcus neoformans moves from the lungs to the meninges and brain.
The sinuses and ear canals
Colonizing the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva is typical of Aspergillus, alongside fungal balls in the lungs. Cryptococcus neoformans is feared for spreading to the meninges and brain.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set1.q: A fungus with few, if any, virulence factors causes a systemic infection in a patient taking long-term corticosteroids. How is this mycosis best classified?
opts: Dermatophytosis

Dermatophytoses are strictly confined to keratinized epidermis (skin, hair, scalp and nails), so they are not systemic. A low-virulence fungus causing systemic disease in a patient on corticosteroids is an opportunistic mycosis.
Opportunistic mycosis

Correct. Few, if any, virulence factors plus a host weakened by corticosteroids is the picture of an opportunistic mycosis: these fungi usually start infection in immunocompromised hosts, and predisposing factors such as primary illness, corticosteroid use, diabetes and cancer should be considered.
True (primary) mycosis

A true pathogen can invade and grow in a healthy host and does not depend on a weakened one. A fungus with few, if any, virulence factors striking a patient on corticosteroids is an opportunist; the tell is the impaired host.
Subcutaneous mycosis

Subcutaneous mycoses begin when trauma inoculates the fungus into the skin or nails, a level of invasion rather than a degree of pathogenicity. This infection is systemic and arose in a corticosteroid-weakened host from a low-virulence fungus, which marks it as opportunistic.

mis.Subcutaneous mycosis: level of invasion confused with pathogenicity
mis.Dermatophytosis: superficial skin mycosis confused with systemic disease

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A woman has had several episodes of vaginal yeast infection over the years. Which statement about immunity to opportunistic fungi like this one is accurate?
opts: Healthy people have no defense to them

Humans are relatively resistant to fungi while the immune system is competent: skin, mucous membranes, cilia, cell-mediated immunity, phagocytosis and inflammation all defend. What is missing against opportunists is lasting immunity, so reinfection is likely.
Reinfection with them is highly likely

Correct. Long-term immunity does not develop against opportunistic fungi, so reinfection with them is highly likely; repeated episodes of vaginal yeast infection or foot fungus are the familiar result. The same fact, that reinfection is exceedingly common, is why immunization against fungi is typically ineffective.
One episode leaves lasting immunity

Long-term immunity does not follow infection with opportunistic fungi; reinfection is highly likely, which is why her episodes keep recurring. The recurrence itself is the tell that no protective immunity formed.
Vaccination prevents further episodes
Immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections precisely because reinfection is exceedingly common. Control relies on antifungal drugs such as azoles and nystatin, not on vaccines.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A kidney transplant recipient has cough, fever, shallow respiration and cyanosis. A tissue section shows the cysts seen here, each containing several bodies. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Cryptococcus neoformans

Cryptococcus neoformans appears as an encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain and causes cough, fever and lung nodules before spreading to the meninges. Cysts each holding several bodies identify Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Aspergillus fumigatus
Aspergillus grows as branched septate hyphae with conidial heads and forms fungal balls in the lungs. Rounded cysts containing several bodies, not hyphae, point to Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Blastomyces dermatitidis

Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic true pathogen whose inhaled conidia become yeasts in the lungs, at times mistaken for lung cancer on chest X-ray. Cysts holding several bodies in a transplant recipient point to Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Pneumocystis jirovecii

Correct. Cysts containing several bodies are the tissue form of Pneumocystis jirovecii, a small, unicellular fungus. Kidney transplant patients are at high risk, and cough, fever, shallow respiration and cyanosis are its pneumonia, in which secretions block breathing.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Blastomyces dermatitidis lives in forest soil, decaying wood and animal manure. How do people usually acquire it?
opts: By eating crops grown in it
Ingestion is the route of fungal toxins (mycotoxicoses such as aflatoxin from grains, corn and peanuts), not of Blastomyces. Its conidia are inhaled and convert to yeasts in the lungs.
By inhaling its conidia

Correct. People inhale the conidia when the soil is disturbed; the inhaled conidia (10 to 100) convert to yeasts and multiply in the lungs, causing cough, chest pain and fever. Chronic skin nodules and later bone and nervous system complications can follow.
From an infected person's cough
Most fungal pathogens do not need a host to complete their life cycles, so their infections are generally not communicable. Blastomyces is acquired from its soil habitat by inhaling conidia.
Through sexual contact
Sexual contact is one way Candida albicans spreads, a yeast of the human body, not a soil fungus like Blastomyces dermatitidis. Its conidia are inhaled from soil, decaying wood or manure.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which factors may have contributed to the rise of mucormycosis in India?
opts: Steroid misuse and uncontrolled diabetes

Correct. Mucormycosis has become a big concern in India over the last few years, and injudicious use of respiratory steroids and uncontrolled diabetes may have contributed. Rhino-orbital-oral-cerebral disease has been documented.
Agricultural spraying of azole fungicides

Crop spraying is blamed for azole resistance in Aspergillus, a different airborne soil fungus. The rise of mucormycosis in India is linked to injudicious respiratory steroid use and uncontrolled diabetes.
Contaminated contact lenses in the eye
Contaminated contact lenses let Fusarium, a mainly tropical soil mold, infect the eye. Mucormycosis in India is tied to respiratory steroids used injudiciously and to uncontrolled diabetes.
Damp buildings harboring toxic mold

Damp buildings are linked to Stachybotrys chartarum and sick building syndrome, which carries a black mold nickname but is very different from mucormycosis. In India, steroid misuse and uncontrolled diabetes are the suspected contributors.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which fungus causes the disease nicknamed 'Ohio Valley fever'?
opts: Coccidioides immitis

Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis, 'Valley fever' without the Ohio, mainly in the southwestern United States extending to Mexico and Central and South America. 'Ohio Valley fever' is histoplasmosis.
Blastomyces dermatitidis

Blastomyces dermatitidis causes North American blastomycosis, its own name, in the midwestern and southeastern United States and southern Canada. 'Ohio Valley fever' is the nickname of histoplasmosis.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis is endemic in Central and South America, the rarest of the primary mycoses, with no Ohio connection. 'Ohio Valley fever' is histoplasmosis, from Histoplasma capsulatum.
Histoplasma capsulatum

Correct. Histoplasmosis, 'Ohio Valley fever', is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, the most common true fungal pathogen. It is known in the eastern and central United States and is now recognized as endemic in parts of Latin America and Africa.

mis.Blastomyces dermatitidis: nickname given to a neighboring endemic fungus

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A gardener has the forearm lesions shown, which began as a single nodule where a thorn pierced the hand. Which organism most likely caused them?
opts: Malassezia furfur

Malassezia furfur is the yeast of tinea versicolor, a superficial mycosis with mild, chronic scaling and mottling of the skin rather than nodules. A thorn wound followed by a nodule and spreading lesions marks Sporothrix schenckii.
Candida albicans

Cutaneous candidiasis develops in chronically moist skin, such as the armpits, groin and under the breasts, and in burn patients; a thorn does not plant it. A nodule at a puncture site that spreads to nearby lymph nodes is Sporothrix schenckii.
Sporothrix schenckii

Correct. A thorn puncture, a nodule at the entry site, then a line of lesions up the forearm is lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis: Sporothrix schenckii forms a nodule where contaminated plant material penetrated the skin and spreads to nearby lymph nodes.
Trichophyton species

Trichophyton is a dermatophyte: tinea corporis forms inflamed, red rings on smooth skin after contact with people, clothing or bedding, and stays in keratinized epidermis. A nodule at a thorn prick that spreads toward the lymph nodes is subcutaneous sporotrichosis.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which three genera cause ringworm?
opts: Trichosporon, Piedraia, Malassezia

These are the agents of the superficial mycoses: Trichosporon causes white piedra, Piedraia black piedra, and the yeast Malassezia furfur tinea versicolor despite its tinea name. Ringworm comes from Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton.
Rhizopus, Mucor, Fusarium

Rhizopus and Mucor cause mucormycosis, and Fusarium infects eyes, toenails, feet and burned skin; all three are opportunists of compromised hosts. Ringworm is caused by the dermatophyte genera Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton.
Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides

These are true fungal pathogens, caught by inhaling conidia from disturbed soil and causing lung disease that can become systemic. Ringworm is a cutaneous mycosis caused by Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton.
Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton

Correct. The dermatophytes belong to the genera Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton. They are closely related and morphologically similar to one another, and the actual causative agent of ringworm (tinea) varies from case to case.

mis.Trichosporon, Piedraia, Malassezia: superficial mycosis agents (tinea versicolor name trap)

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which drugs are common treatment options for Pneumocystis pneumonia?
opts: Pentamidine and co-trimoxazole

Correct. Pentamidine, an antiprotozoal, and the antibacterial co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) are common treatment options, and neither is a traditional antifungal drug. Without such medication the pneumonia can be rapidly fatal.
Amphotericin B and azoles

Amphotericin B and azoles are traditional antifungals, used for systemic candidiasis and, as amphotericin B with an azole, for cryptococcosis. Pneumocystis pneumonia is unusual: it is treated with pentamidine and co-trimoxazole, which are not traditional antifungals.
Topical azoles for several weeks
Topical azoles for several weeks treat dermatophytoses of the skin, hair and nails. Pneumocystis pneumonia fills the lungs with secretions and is treated with pentamidine or co-trimoxazole.
Tissue removal and amphotericin B

Removal of affected tissues plus amphotericin B is the treatment for mucormycosis invading the nose, eyes, heart and brain. Pneumocystis pneumonia is treated medically with pentamidine and co-trimoxazole.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which conditions promote dermatophyte infection?
opts: Corticosteroids and diabetes

Corticosteroids, diabetes and other impaired defenses predispose to the opportunistic mycoses, such as candidiasis and cryptococcosis. Dermatophyte infection is promoted instead by hardy spores, abraded skin and close contact with people or fomites.
Inhaling dust from disturbed soil

Dust from disturbed soil carries the conidia of the true fungal pathogens into the lungs. Dermatophytes are not inhaled; their hardy spores infect abraded skin through close contact with people or fomites.
Puncture wounds from plant thorns

A thorn puncture carries subcutaneous fungi such as Sporothrix schenckii into deeper tissue. Dermatophytes stay in keratinized epidermis and spread by close contact with people or fomites onto abraded skin.
Abraded skin and close contact

Correct. Hardy dermatophyte spores, abraded skin and close person-to-person or person-to-fomite contact promote infection. The natural reservoirs are humans, animals and soil, and shared items such as exercise equipment can carry the fungus from one person to the next.
set2.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 12, 22, 24, 39 and 43

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Besides the lungs, which sites can Aspergillus colonize?
opts: Pubic and axillary hair shafts
Whitish masses on pubic and axillary hair shafts are white piedra, caused by Trichosporon. Aspergillus, an airborne fungus, colonizes the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva.
Lymph nodes near a thorn wound
Lymph nodes near a puncture wound are reached by Sporothrix schenckii in lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis. Aspergillus colonizes the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva besides the lungs.
Moist skin folds under breasts

Moist skin folds under the breasts, in the armpits and in the groin are where intertriginous Candida lesions form in obese patients. Aspergillus colonizes the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva.
Sinuses, ear canals, eyelids

Correct. Aspergillus infection usually occurs in the lungs, but the fungus can also colonize the sinuses, ear canals, eyelids and conjunctiva. Invasive disease goes further, to the brain, heart and other organs.
set2.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 39, 49, 54 and 60

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which treatment is commonly used for systemic candidiasis?
opts: Topical antifungals alone

Topical antifungals are used for superficial Candida infections such as skin irritation, not for systemic disease. A systemic infection in a seriously compromised host calls for amphotericin B and azoles.
Pentamidine and co-trimoxazole

Pentamidine and co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) treat Pneumocystis pneumonia and are not traditional antifungal drugs. Systemic candidiasis is treated with antifungals, amphotericin B and azoles.
Ultraviolet light treatment
Ultraviolet light treatments, like debridement, have helped in dermatophytoses of keratinized skin. Systemic candidiasis is a deep, potentially fatal infection treated with amphotericin B and azoles.
Amphotericin B and azoles

Correct. Topical antifungals are used for superficial Candida infections, while amphotericin B and azoles are commonly used for systemic infections. Systemic candidiasis is the overwhelming, potentially fatal form seen in seriously compromised hosts.
set2.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 45, 52, 55 and 58

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which weather pattern most enhances the spread of Coccidioides?
opts: Steady rain through winter and spring

Coccidioides remains dormant in winter and spring, so steady seasonal rain is not its spreading pattern. Its spread is driven by cycles of drought and heavy rain followed by windstorms that lift spore-laden dust.
Cool, humid conditions year-round

Cool, humid soils are the setting of Paracoccidioides in Central and South America. Coccidioides belongs to hot, semiarid climates with alkaline, salty soil, spread by drought, heavy rain and windstorms.
Drought, then heavy rain, then windstorms

Correct. Coccidioides lives in alkaline, salty soils of semiarid, hot climates, and its spread is greatly enhanced by cycles of drought and heavy rains followed by windstorms that raise spore-laden dust. It remains dormant in winter and spring.
Cold, wet weather after a warm, dry spell

Sporulation in colder, wetter weather after a warm, dry dormancy is the pattern of Blastomyces dermatitidis in the midwestern and southeastern United States. Coccidioides spreads with drought, heavy rain and then windstorms.

mis.Steady rain through winter and spring: dormant season taken for active season

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: True fungal pathogens occur in predictable geographic patterns. What do these patterns ultimately follow?
opts: Human population density
These fungi live free in soil and need no host to complete their life cycles, so the crowding of people does not set their range. Their endemic regions coincide with climate and soil requirements.
Travel routes of infected people
Infections by most fungal pathogens are not communicable, so infected travelers do not carry an endemic zone with them. The zones coincide with the climate and soil each fungus requires.
Bird and bat migration routes

Bird and bat guano enriches the soil Histoplasma grows in, but the pattern of the true pathogens as a group follows climate and soil requirements, not animal migration; Coccidioides, for example, needs alkaline, salty, semiarid soil.
Climate and soil requirements

Correct. True fungal pathogens are distributed in predictable geographical patterns that ultimately coincide with climate and soil requirements, so each is restricted to certain endemic regions; Coccidioides, for example, lives in alkaline, salty soils of hot, semiarid climates.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: In the laboratory workup of hair, skin and nail specimens for fungi, which method is applied directly to the hairs?
opts: Inoculation of animals

Animal inoculation is reserved for diagnosing systemic mycoses when other methods are unavailable or indeterminate, not for hair, skin or nail specimens. Hairs are examined directly under Wood's light.
Examination under Wood's light

Correct. For hair, skin and nail specimens the identification pathway uses Wood's light on the hairs, alongside a hot potassium hydroxide wet mount, brighteners and periodic acid-Schiff staining, before culture on selective media for 4 weeks and a hair infection test.
Negative stain for a capsule
A negative stain for a capsule is used on sputum to show encapsulated yeasts such as Cryptococcus; it is not the direct examination of hairs. Hairs are examined under Wood's light.
Germ tube test in serum

The germ tube test identifies yeasts that sprout hyphal tubes after 2 to 4 hours in serum, among the tests for blood, cerebrospinal fluid, pus and vaginal secretion isolates. Hairs are examined directly under Wood's light.
set2.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, image on Slide 17

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which pair of fungi both sit in the World Health Organization's critical priority group?
opts: Aspergillus fumigatus and Fusarium
Aspergillus fumigatus is critical (third on the list), but Fusarium species are in the high priority group, with Histoplasma and the Mucorales. Both Candida albicans and Candida auris are critical.
Cryptococcus neoformans and C. gattii

Cryptococcus neoformans is critical, number one on the list, but Cryptococcus gattii is medium priority, with Coccidioides, Pneumocystis jirovecii and Paracoccidioides. The same genus does not mean the same tier.
Candida albicans and Candida auris

Correct. The critical priority group of the World Health Organization's fungal priority pathogens list is Cryptococcus neoformans, Aspergillus fumigatus, Candida albicans and Candida auris. Both Candida species named here are in it; other Candida species sit one tier lower, in the high group.
Candida auris and Histoplasma

Candida auris is critical, but Histoplasma species are in the high priority group, with other Candida species, Fusarium, the eumycetoma agents and the Mucorales. The fully critical pair here is Candida albicans with Candida auris.

mis.Candida auris and Histoplasma: one member from the high tier
mis.Aspergillus fumigatus and Fusarium: one member from the high tier
mis.Cryptococcus neoformans and C. gattii: same genus assumed to share a tier

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A patient receiving amphotericin B develops fever, weakness and an arrhythmia. Why does this drug also harm the patient's own cells?
opts: Its target is a cell wall humans share

Humans have no such cell wall; the thicker fungal cell wall is what human cells lack, which is why potassium hydroxide lyses human cells and spares fungi. The drug acts on membrane lipids, which fungal and human cells, both eukaryotic, have in common.
It comes from a fungus, not a bacterium

Amphotericin B is produced by a soil bacterium, Streptomyces, and its source is not what makes it toxic. The toxicity comes from its non-selective action on the membranes of eukaryotic cells, fungal and human alike.
It destroys the patient's normal flora

Loss of normal flora is not the cause given for its toxicity; fever, weakness and arrhythmia are direct side effects. Amphotericin B attacks membrane lipids in eukaryotic cells, human as well as fungal.
Fungi and humans are both eukaryotes

Correct. Amphotericin B complexes with cell membrane lipids, and because fungi and humans are both eukaryotes the action is not selective enough to attack only fungi. Fatigue, weakness, fever and arrhythmia are its potentially serious side effects, hence the nickname 'ampho-terrible'.

mis.Its target is a cell wall humans share: assumes humans have a cell wall

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Under the microscope, a hair from a patient's scalp carries the dark, gritty nodule shown. What is this infection?
opts: Tinea capitis

Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair-bearing head that may cause hair loss and is common in children. A discrete gritty nodule stuck to the hair shaft is black piedra, a superficial mycosis.
Tinea versicolor
Tinea versicolor is a skin infection by the yeast Malassezia furfur, with mild, chronic scaling and mottling. A nodule on a hair shaft, not a change in the skin, marks black piedra.
Black piedra

Correct. Black piedra, caused by Piedraia species, forms dark-brown to black gritty nodules mainly on scalp hairs, as on this hair shaft. It is considered non-contagious, may follow poor hygiene and is not common in the United States.
White piedra
White piedra, caused by Trichosporon, forms whitish or colored masses mainly on pubic or axillary hair. A dark, gritty nodule on a scalp hair is black piedra, caused by Piedraia.
set2.cite: PAJ5200.Fungi of Medical importance.pptx, Slide 44 and 49 and image on Slide 50

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Which effects characterize aflatoxin, the toxin found on grains, corn and peanuts?
opts: Hepatotoxic and carcinogenic

Correct. Aflatoxin, found on grains, corn and peanuts, is hepatotoxic and carcinogenic. It is lethal to poultry and livestock, especially turkeys, ducklings, pigs and calves, and in humans it may be a co-factor in liver cancer.
Mind-altering, like lysergic acid

Mind-altering lysergic acid is linked to ergot, found on rye and other grains contaminated by Claviceps fungi. Aflatoxin's harm falls on the liver: it is hepatotoxic, carcinogenic and a possible co-factor in liver cancer.
Hematologic and neurological harm
Severe hematologic and neurological damage is attributed to Stachybotrys chartarum, the black mold of sick building syndrome. Aflatoxin from grains, corn and peanuts is hepatotoxic and carcinogenic.
Hypersensitivity of the lungs
Lung hypersensitivity, as in farmer's lung, is an atopic allergy to fungal spores rather than a toxin effect. Aflatoxin is a fungal toxin that is hepatotoxic and carcinogenic.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: Why are opportunistic mycoses described as an emerging medical concern?
opts: A once-effective vaccine has stopped working

There is no effective fungal vaccine to fail: immunization is typically ineffective against fungal infections because reinfection is exceedingly common. What makes opportunists an emerging concern is their rising share of nosocomial infections.
Spores are newly widespread in the air

Molds and yeasts are already widely distributed in air, dust, fomites and the normal flora of humans, plants and animals, so exposure is nothing new. The change is a rising share of nosocomial infections in hosts with impaired defenses.
Their share of nosocomial infections is rising

Correct. Mycoses account for a growing share of nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections, about one in ten and rising, which is why opportunistic fungi are an emerging concern. They need impaired host defenses (human immunodeficiency virus infection, cancer, diabetes, autoimmune disorders) and cause illness from superficial colonization to fatal systemic disease.
Healthy people now catch them easily

Opportunists have little or no virulence of their own and need impaired host defenses; people with a competent immune system are relatively resistant to fungi. The emerging concern is their rising share of nosocomial infections.

set2.q: Which regimen does systemic cryptococcal infection generally require?
opts: Heat packs plus potassium iodide

Heat packs and/or super-saturated potassium iodide treat sporotrichosis of the appendages and lungs, a subcutaneous mycosis. Systemic cryptococcosis, which can reach the brain, needs amphotericin B and an azole such as fluconazole.
Topical azoles for weeks

Topical azoles applied for several weeks are the usual treatment for dermatophytoses of keratinized skin, hair and nails. A systemic infection such as cryptococcosis needs amphotericin B with fluconazole or another azole.
Amphotericin B plus an azole

Correct. Systemic cryptococcal infection generally requires amphotericin B and fluconazole or another azole-type drug. Treatment protocols are well established for patients with human immunodeficiency virus infection, though the drugs may be unavailable in many countries.
Pentamidine plus co-trimoxazole

Pentamidine, an antiprotozoal, and co-trimoxazole, an antibacterial, treat Pneumocystis pneumonia and are not traditional antifungals. Cryptococcosis is treated with the antifungals amphotericin B and fluconazole or another azole.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: How do people usually acquire Aspergillus infection of the lungs?
opts: Breathing in airborne spores

Correct. Aspergillus is a very common airborne soil fungus, and infection usually occurs in the lungs, where its spores germinate and form fungal balls. People at serious risk include those with human immunodeficiency virus infection, leukemia or a transplant.
Thorn or wood puncture wounds
A thorn or wood puncture carries Sporothrix schenckii into the skin, where it forms a nodule and spreads to nearby lymph nodes. Aspergillus is airborne, and its spores germinate in the lungs.
Childbirth and breast-feeding

Childbirth and breast-feeding, along with surgery and sexual contact, spread Candida albicans from person to person. Aspergillus comes from the air and soil; its spores reach the lungs and germinate there.
Contact with public surfaces
Public surfaces spread tinea pedis and tinea manuum, ringworm of the foot and hand. Aspergillus infection begins in the lungs, where its airborne spores germinate.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A man is hospitalized with disseminated histoplasmosis, and his wife asks whether she could catch it from him. What is accurate?
opts: She cannot catch it from him

Correct. Histoplasmosis is not transmitted person to person. People acquire it by inhaling conidia from moist soil enriched with bird or bat guano, and in the body the fungus lives as a yeast inside phagocytes, not as an infective spore.
She could inhale spores he coughs
The infective forms are conidia from soil; in the lungs the fungus lives as a yeast inside phagocytes. Histoplasmosis is not transmitted person to person, so his cough does not pass it on.
She could catch it from his skin

Skin-to-skin and fomite spread belong to dermatophytes and Candida, which naturally inhabit the human body. Histoplasmosis is not transmitted person to person by any route; it is caught by inhaling conidia from soil.
She could if her immunity is weak

A weakened immune system raises the risk of severe fungal disease, but it does not create a person-to-person route: histoplasmosis is not transmitted between people at all, whatever the contact's immune status.

set2.q: These two colonies are the same fungal pathogen grown on agar below 35 C (left) and at 37 C (right). Which property of the fungus do they demonstrate?
opts: Thermal dimorphism

Correct. One fungus forming a fuzzy, mold-like colony below 35 C and a different, yeast-like colony at 37 C, human body temperature, is thermal dimorphism: multicellular mold at the lower temperature, unicellular yeast at 37 C. Histoplasma capsulatum, the most common true fungal pathogen, shows exactly this.
Germ tube formation

A germ tube is a tiny hyphal tube that some yeasts sprout after 2 to 4 hours in serum; it is read under the microscope, not as two colonies at two temperatures. Here the only variable is temperature, which is how dimorphism is demonstrated.
Capsule production

A capsule is a virulence factor shown by a negative stain of the cells, as with encapsulated budding yeast, not by comparing colonies grown at two temperatures. The change in colony form between below 35 C and 37 C is thermal dimorphism.
Spherule formation

Spherules are giant sporangia full of endospores that Coccidioides forms in the lungs; they are seen in tissue, not as a colony on a plate. Two colony forms at two temperatures show thermal dimorphism.

set2.q: A vaginal swab is treated with dilute potassium hydroxide before microscopy for yeast. What does this step accomplish?
opts: Lyses human cells, leaving fungal cells intact

Correct. Dilute potassium hydroxide lyses human epithelial cells but leaves fungal cells intact, because fungi have a thicker cell wall that human cells lack. What remains under the microscope is the fungus, for example germinating Candida albicans.
Lyses fungal cells, leaving human cells intact
This is reversed: fungi survive potassium hydroxide because of their thicker cell wall, while human epithelial cells, which lack that wall, are lysed. The step clears away human cells, not fungi.
Outlines the yeast capsule by negative staining

A negative stain is a separate step, used for example on sputum to show encapsulated budding yeast such as Cryptococcus. Potassium hydroxide does not stain anything; it dissolves human epithelial cells.
Induces yeasts to sprout germ tubes

Germ tubes sprout when some yeasts are incubated in serum for 2 to 4 hours, a separate identification test. Potassium hydroxide instead dissolves human epithelial cells so the fungal cells can be seen.

set2.q: Which person fits the risk profile for paracoccidioidomycosis?
opts: Older road worker in desert dust

Increasing age and occupational dust exposure, as in road construction, are risk factors for Coccidioides in hot, semiarid climates. Paracoccidioides strikes poorly nourished male farm workers over 40 in cool, humid Central and South America.
Poorly nourished male farm worker over 40

Correct. In the cool, humid soils of Central and South America, rural farm workers and harvesters are most at risk; poor nutrition is a predisposing factor, and male sex and age over 40 add to the risk. All of those clues are present here.
Shoeless male farmer aged 11 to 30
A male farmer aged 11 to 30 who goes without shoes fits the eumycetoma profile, deep tissue infections of poor countries. Paracoccidioidomycosis strikes poorly nourished rural farm workers over 40.
Rose gardener with a thorn puncture
A thorn puncture in a gardener is the classic route of sporotrichosis, 'rose-gardener's disease'. The paracoccidioidomycosis profile is a poorly nourished male farm worker over 40.

set2.q: After a presumptive diagnosis of candidiasis, how are the Candida species told apart?
opts: A potassium hydroxide mount

A potassium hydroxide mount lyses human epithelial cells and leaves the thicker-walled fungal cells intact, showing that fungus is present. It reveals the yeast, but growth on selective, differential media is what differentiates the Candida species.
Selective, differential media

Correct. A presumptive diagnosis rests on budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae, but growth on selective, differential media differentiates the Candida species. The smear shows a Candida infection; culture on these media names the species.
A negative stain for a capsule
A negative stain demonstrates the capsule of an encapsulated budding yeast, the sign of Cryptococcus neoformans. Candida species are told apart by growth on selective, differential media.
Wood's light on infected hairs
Wood's light on hairs is a step in working up hair, skin and nail specimens, the territory of the dermatophytes. Candida species are separated by growth on selective, differential media.

set2.q: A 9-year-old has the scaly patch shown, with hair lost over it. Which name fits this ringworm?
opts: Tinea versicolor

Tinea versicolor, despite its name, is a superficial mycosis caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur, with mild, chronic scaling and mottling of the skin. Scalp ringworm with hair loss in a child is tinea capitis, a dermatophytosis.
Tinea capitis

Correct. Ringworm of the scalp, tinea capitis, affects the scalp and hair-bearing regions of the head; hair may be lost, and it is common in children. The child's age, the scalp location and the hair loss over the lesion all fit.
Tinea barbae

Tinea barbae is ringworm of the chin and beard of adult males, contracted mainly from animals, so a child's age already argues against it. A scaly patch on the scalp with hair loss in a child is tinea capitis.
Tinea corporis

Tinea corporis forms inflamed, red ring lesions anywhere on smooth skin and spreads by contact, clothing and bedding. The hair-bearing scalp of a child, with hair loss, is the territory of tinea capitis.

set2.q: Which methods are the best tools for diagnosing cryptococcosis?
opts: Biochemical and serological tests

Correct. For cryptococcosis, biochemical and serological testing are the best diagnostic tools. A negative stain can demonstrate the encapsulated budding yeast, and systemic infection generally requires amphotericin B with fluconazole or another azole.
Inoculation of laboratory animals
Animal inoculation is performed only to help diagnose systemic mycoses when other methods are unavailable or indeterminate. For cryptococcosis, the best tools are biochemical and serological tests.
Wood's light examination of hair
Wood's light is used on hairs when working up hair, skin and nail specimens. Cryptococcosis, a lung and meningeal infection, is best diagnosed by biochemical and serological tests.
A chest X-ray showing lung nodules

A chest X-ray can mislead: Blastomyces multiplying in the lungs may be mistaken for lung cancer on it. Cryptococcus also causes lung nodules, but biochemical and serological tests are the best tools for diagnosis.

set2.q: A 58-year-old African-American man who repairs roads in the southwestern United States develops a lung infection after a dust storm. Which fungus is the most likely cause?
opts: Blastomyces dermatitidis

Blastomyces lives in forest soil, decaying wood and manure in the midwestern and southeastern United States and southern Canada, not in southwestern desert dust. The setting and risk factors fit Coccidioides.
Paracoccidioides brasiliensis
Paracoccidioides lives in cool, humid soils of Central and South America and strikes poorly nourished rural farm workers. A southwestern United States road worker exposed to dust fits Coccidioides.
Coccidioides immitis

Correct. The southwestern United States, road repair and a dust storm are classic exposures for Coccidioides immitis (Valley fever), and African or African-American descent, increasing age (over 40 to 60 years) and occupational dust exposure are its significant risk factors. Inhaled arthrospores establish the lung infection.
Histoplasma capsulatum

Histoplasma is acquired from moist, nitrogen-rich soil with bird and bat guano and is known in the eastern and central United States. Southwestern dust, road work and these risk factors point to Coccidioides.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of fungi of medical importance
set2.q: A man with diabetes has the thick, white, adherent growth on the tongue shown. Which finding in a scraping would support a presumptive diagnosis?
opts: Cysts containing several bodies

Cysts containing several bodies are the tissue form of Pneumocystis jirovecii, a cause of pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts. Thrush is a Candida albicans infection, supported by budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae.
Budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae

Correct. A thick, white, adherent growth on the mucous membranes of the mouth in a man with diabetes is thrush, from Candida albicans. A presumptive diagnosis is made when budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae are found; growth on selective, differential media then tells the Candida species apart.
Encapsulated yeast on negative stain

An encapsulated budding yeast on negative stain identifies Cryptococcus neoformans, which infects the lungs and meninges. Thrush on the tongue is Candida albicans, presumptively diagnosed by budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae.
Branched septate hyphae in sputum

Branched septate hyphae, as seen in a sputum specimen, point to Aspergillus, whose spores form fungal balls in the lungs. A white oral growth calls for Candida's own finding: budding yeast cells and pseudohyphae.
